seoDescription: Learn how to build a powerful AI agent with Flowise v3. This tutorial guides you through creating an assistant that can perform web searches using SERP API, answer questions from a custom knowledge base, and integrate with external systems like Gmail via Composio to perform actions. We cover setting up a document store, upserting data into a PostgreSQL database via Supabase, managing stale data with a record manager, and configuring tools for a seamless agent experience with OpenAI models.

chapters.title: Demo: AI Agent with Search, Knowledge & Actions
chapters.description: See a demonstration of a Flowise v3 AI agent that can query a knowledge base, search the web, and send emails.

chapters.title: Creating the Agent and Adding Web Search
chapters.description: Create a new agent flow, configure the OpenAI model and system prompt, and add the SERP API tool to enable web search capabilities.

chapters.title: Testing the Agent and Adding a DateTime Tool
chapters.description: Test the web search tool, inspect the process flow, and add the current datetime tool to prevent issues from the model's knowledge cutoff.

chapters.title: Introducing Flowise Document Stores
chapters.description: Learn about the powerful Document Store feature in Flowise for managing custom knowledge bases and preparing documents for ingestion.

chapters.title: Setting Up a PostgreSQL Vector Database with Supabase
chapters.description: Walk through the process of setting up OpenAI embeddings and a free PostgreSQL vector database using Supabase for your document store.

chapters.title: Upserting Data with the Record Manager
chapters.description: Configure the PostgreSQL Record Manager to handle data syncing, upsert documents into the vector store, and see how it prevents duplicates.

chapters.title: Connecting the Knowledge Base to the Agent
chapters.description: Integrate the newly created document store into the agent as a tool and provide a description to guide the agent on when to use it.

chapters.title: Integrating Actions with Composio and Gmail
chapters.description: Add the Composio tool to connect to external systems and walk through setting up a new Gmail integration in the Composio dashboard.

chapters.title: Configuring and Testing the Email Action
chapters.description: Configure the Composio tool in Flowwise to use the Gmail "send email" action and test the agent's ability to send an email.

chapters.title: Conclusion & Future Topics
chapters.description: Recap the agent's capabilities and get a preview of upcoming videos on multi-agent teams and state management in Flowise.

summary:
## Core Agent Components

In Flowise v3, an AI agent is built around a central **Agent** node. This node is then enhanced by adding various **Tools**, which grant the agent new capabilities.

- **LLM**: The core reasoning engine. The tutorial uses **OpenAI's GPT-4 Mini**.
- **System Prompt**: Defines the agent's role, personality, and instructions (e.g., "You are a friendly AI assistant").
- **Tools**: These are add-ons that allow the agent to perform specific tasks beyond generating text. The key tools used are:
    - **Web Search**: To access real-time information from the internet.
    - **Knowledge Base**: To answer questions from a private collection of documents.
    - **External Actions**: To interact with other software, like sending an email.
    - **DateTime**: To provide the agent with the current date and time.

## Managing a Custom Knowledge Base

Flowise's **Document Stores** provide a streamlined way to manage and query private data.

### 1. Creating a Document Store
- Start by creating a new Document Store and giving it a descriptive name.
- Use **Document Loaders** to add content from various sources (e.g., `.docx`, `.csv`, web scrapers).
- Configure a **Text Splitter** (like `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter`) to break large documents into smaller, manageable chunks for the LLM.

### 2. Vector Database Setup (Supabase + PostgreSQL)
- Preparing documents is not enough; they must be "upserted" into a **vector database**.
- The tutorial uses a free **PostgreSQL** database from **Supabase**.

> [!TIP]
> You only need to set up the database and credentials in Flowise once. This configuration can be reused across multiple document stores and agents.

### 3. The Record Manager
- The **Record Manager** is a critical component configured during the first upsert process.
- Its primary job is to track all the data chunks in your vector store.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The Record Manager automatically prevents **duplicate data** on subsequent upserts and handles the removal of **stale data** if you delete a source file and re-upsert. This simplifies data lifecycle management immensely.

### 4. Connecting to the Agent
- To use the knowledge base, add it as a tool in the **Document Store** section of your agent node.
- Provide a **clear description** for the tool (e.g., "Returns documents related to the Oak and Barrel") so the agent knows when to use it.

## Integrating with External Systems

### Web Search (SERP API)
- The **SERP API** tool gives the agent the ability to perform a Google search.
- You can get a free API key from `serpapi.com`.

### External Actions (Composio)
- **Composio** is a powerful tool that acts as a bridge to hundreds of external applications.
- To use it, you need a **Composio API key** and to set up integrations in the Composio dashboard.
- **Example Workflow (Gmail):**
    1. Add the **Composio** tool to your Flowise agent.
    2. In the Composio dashboard, find the **Gmail** app and set up a new **OAuth 2** integration, authorizing it with your Google account.
    3. Back in Flowise, refresh the Composio tool settings.
    4. Select **Gmail** as the app and choose the specific **actions** you want to enable, such as `send_email`.
transcription:
## Demo: AI Agent with Search, Knowledge & Actions

Flowise makes it super easy to build AI agents. And with the release of version 3, it just got way simpler. In fact, what you're looking at here is everything you need to build an agent that's able to answer questions from a custom knowledge base, go online and perform a Google search, and perform actions on external systems like sending email. So, let's see this in action.

We can open up the chat, and I'm actually going to expand this, and let's ask a question from our own custom knowledge base. And for this demo, I uploaded several information related to our fictitious restaurant. This includes the menu items along with their prices. So, for example, let's ask what the cost of a ribeye steak is. What is the cost of a ribeye steak at the Oak and Barrel?

And indeed, we get the correct answer back along with the citations. And we can see the knowledge base was indeed accessed. And by the way, managing knowledge bases in Flowise is incredibly simple. When we go to document stores, we can create a document store, which is effectively a knowledge base, and simply upload and remove documents whenever we want to make changes. That's it. We don't have to build any complex workflows for managing things like stale data and avoiding duplicate records. We will get back to this in this tutorial.

So, let's go back to our agent. Let's get our agent to perform a web search. So, let's ask who won the 2025 Oscars. And here we can see the web search tool was indeed called. And we get the best actor, actress, supporting actor, and supporting actress. And doing a quick Google search, this does seem to be correct.

Let's get our agent to send an email. Let's say email these results to leonfansv@gmail.com. Let's send this. And now we can see the Gmail send tool was called and our agent is saying the email was sent. Looking at my emails, I did receive an email with the 2025 Oscar winners and this includes all the information extracted by the agent.

## Creating the Agent and Adding Web Search

I mean, this could not be any easier to use. So in this video, I'll show you how to build AI agents using Flowwise, which includes a custom knowledge base, web search, as well as integration to external systems.

First, let's create our agent flow. Within agent flows, let's create a new agent flow and ensure you've got version two selected. Let's create our flow and let's give it a name like AI agent. Then from add nodes, let's add our agent node like so. And let's double click on this agent. I'm going to give mine a name like my assistant. For the model, I'm going to select chat OpenAI. I'll select my OpenAI credentials. And for the model name, I'll simply leave it on GPT-4 Mini. Great.

Under messages, I'm going to add a system message. And here I'll define a role. Let's expand this and let's just say you are a friendly AI assistant. Answer the user's questions in a friendly and helpful manner. Let's save this. I'm going to close these parameters and let's scroll down. And here you will find the section for tools and this is where we can add things like calculators, integration with external systems, web search, etc.

We want to give our agent the ability to answer questions from the web. So let's start by adding a web search tool. Under tools, let's search for SERP API. And then under SERP API parameters, click on credentials and click on create new. Let's give this a name like SERP API. And for the API key, go to serpapi.com and sign into your account. This is free to use. Simply copy your API key and add it to flowwise. Let's click add. And that should be all we need for this tool. You will also notice the section called require human input. This means before the agent calls this tool, it will first ask the user's permission to do so. I'll simply leave this off for now.

## Testing the Agent and Adding a DateTime Tool

Let's test this by closing this popup. Let's save the flow. And in the chat, let's ask something like who won the 2025 Oscars. And what you will see here is that the search tool was indeed called and we did get the correct answer back. We can click on the tool icon to see more information about calling this tool. We can see the input that was passed from our agent to this tool and this is basically the search term that was used when performing this Google search. And we also get the output from that tool.

If we expand process flow, we can also see some additional information by expanding this My Assistant node. And at the top, we can see all the available tools to the agent. At the moment, we only have one. And scrolling down, we can see the system prompt for the agent. We can see the user's question. And then we can see the assistant decided to call the SERP API tool. This block shows the results from that tool call. And then finally we get the answer from the agent.

There is another tool that I like to add to my agents and that is the datetime tool because if we ask the agent what is the current date and time the agent will say that it's actually April 4th 2024. That is based on when the training data cutoff was for this agent. And sometimes this can affect the behavior of the assistant. So when we ask it to perform some research, it might use the wrong date in its search query. In fact, if you try the Oscar scenario, it might even tell you that the 2025 Oscars haven't taken place yet. That's because the agent believes it's still 2024. So if we go to add tools and in this list, we can search for current date and time. And now if we save this flow and test this again by asking what is the current date, we can see the current date and time tool was called and we are now getting the correct answer. Awesome.

## Introducing Flowise Document Stores

Now let's have a look at adding a custom knowledge base to our assistant. Let's go back to the dashboard and let's go to document stores. And document stores is one of the most impressive features offered by Flowwise. If you've ever tried to work with custom knowledge bases in things like n8n and make.com, you'll know how tricky it can be to keep track of your existing documents, avoid duplicates and stale data. Document stores in Flowise takes care of all of that for you.

So within document stores, let's click on add new. Let's call this Oak and Barrel knowledge base. Let's add this and let's click on our document store. Now let's start adding data to this document store. Let's click on add document loader. And in here you've got access to plenty of document loaders. We can load data from Air Table. We can call APIs, use web scrapers, pull from Confluence, and much much more. I've prepared two files for this demonstration. First is a Word document that contains Q&As about our restaurant. So I'll select that document. Then under text splitters, I can decide how I want to chunk this document. So let's select recursive character text splitter and I'll split this document into chunks based on a 1,000 character chunk size and a 200 character overlap. Let's click on preview chunks. And Flowwise has now broken this document up into five chunks. And we can view the different chunks down here. Cool. Let's process this. And after a second, everything will go green, which means this document has now been prepared and is ready to be upserted into our database.

## Setting Up a PostgreSQL Vector Database with Supabase

And this takes me to a very important point. At this stage, the document store is not ready to be used. At this stage, Flowise simply pulled in the document and it did the necessary preparation on that document. We now need to load this data into a vector database. So, this step might feel tricky, but I promise you it's not that bad, and you only have to do this once. Go to more actions, then click on upsert all chunks.

Now, we have to go through the simple process of setting up the embeddings, the vector database, and finally the record manager. For the embeddings, let's select OpenAI embeddings and let's select our OpenAI credentials and let's select embeddings-3-large as our model. And that's all we have to do for embeddings. For the vector database, we can use any of these providers. We will be using a PostgreSQL database in this series. So let's select PostgreSQL. And now we have to select our PostgreSQL credentials. Let's click on this dropdown. Let's click on create new. And for the name, let's enter PostgreSQL API. And now we have to provide the username and password for our database.

Now we don't yet have a database available. So let's go ahead and set one up. In order to set up a free PostgreSQL database, go to supabase.com and then sign up for an account. From your dashboard, click on new project and let's give it a name like Flowwise v3 Tutorial. Then create a password and do make a note of this password as you will need it later on. Then select your region. I'll select US East. Let's create a new project. Then at the very top click on connect and scroll down to this transaction pooler section and expand the parameters. Now we can copy this username and add it to this field. Also enter the password that you selected earlier. Then click on add. For the host, let's go back to Supabase and copy this host name like so. Let's also copy the database name and add it to Flowwise. And lastly, let's copy the port name and add that to Flowwise as well. For this SSL toggle, I'm going to leave it off. But if you are using the hosted version of Flowwise, I think you might have to enable it. So I would recommend leaving it off. If you run into issues, simply enable it and try again. And we don't have to change anything else on this page. So this vector store will be used to store these chunks or the documents in this database.

## Upserting Data with the Record Manager

The record manager is responsible for keeping track of our data and avoid stale data and duplicates. And also if we delete data from our knowledge base the record manager will ensure that data gets removed from our vector store as well. This is very easy to set up. Again we'll select Postgress record manager. We'll select the Postgress credentials. Then we can simply copy over the host details, the database name and the port number. Let's save this config. And finally let's pick on upsert. Upsert will now take all of those chunks that we created earlier and load our data into the database. And we can see five documents were indeed loaded into the database.

Now check this out. If we click on upsert again, what would happen in other platforms is that the data will simply be duplicated in the database. But because we have record manager set up, Flowwise will intelligently detect that those records already exist in the database and therefore they have been skipped. Now, if you ever want to add or remove data, simply go back to the document store and let's actually upload a CSV file containing all our menu items. So, let's select our menu file. Let's click on preview chunks. And here we can see all this items from the menu. So, I'm going to process this. And now we can see that second file over here. Now, all we have to do is upsert this data. So, under more actions, let's go to upsert all chunks. Let's click on upsert. And if everything goes well, five documents should be skipped and 20 documents from the menu should be inserted, which is exactly what happened. How cool is that?

We can also test our retrieval at this point. So let's click on test retrieval. And now we can mimic the behavior of what would happen if the agent tried to retrieve this data. Let's say rib eye price. Let's run this. And indeed, we get the rib eye price back. Or what about current specials? And great, the first document contains the current specials from the Oaken Barrel. Of course, deleting data is just as simple. Simply delete the document and run the upsert process again. That's it.

## Connecting the Knowledge Base to the Agent

Now, how do we use this document store in our agent flow? That's really easy. Let's go to our agent. Let's double click on our agent node. And scrolling down we can find this document store section. So all we have to do is click on add knowledge from document store. In this dropdown let's select our document store. And now we just have to describe when this document store should be used. So let's say returns documents related to the Oak and Barrel. So if the user asked any questions about the Oak and Barrel, this document store will be used. We can also decide whether or not we want to return the citations. So I'm actually going to enable this and then let's save our flow and let's ask a question like what are the current specials at the Oak and Barrel. Our knowledge base was called and we get the correct answer back along with the supporting documents.

## Integrating Actions with Composio and Gmail

Our agents are also able to integrate with external systems using the Composio tool. For example, let's say we want our agent to be able to send emails on our behalf. Let's do that now. Actually, under tools, let's add the Composio tool. And then within Composio parameters, let's click on credentials and let's click on create new. Let's call this Composio API. And for the API key, head over to Composio.dev. And Composio just makes it very easy for AI systems like Flowwise to integrate with external platforms. And do take note they also offer a Composio MCP server which is also supported by Flowwise.

Go ahead and sign into your account. Then from your dashboard go to settings and under project API keys. Let's add a new API key. Let's call this Flowwise V3 tutorial. Let's copy the key and add it to Flowwise. Let's click on add.

And before we do anything on app name, status or action, we need to set a few things up in Composio. Basically, all we have to do is tell Composio which apps we want to have access to. So, let's go to all apps. And here you will see hundreds of integrations with external systems like Outlook, Google Docs, Air Table, and much much more. Because we want to send emails, we can set up an integration to Gmail. So let's click on Gmail. And on this page, we can see all the actions that are available within this app like the ability to send emails, read emails, etc.

Let's then click on setup Gmail integration. On the left hand side, click on new integration. Select OOTH 2. Then scrolling down, click on create integration. Then click on try connecting default Gmail. You will now be asked to select your email address. So let's do that. Let's click on continue. Let's click on continue again. And that's it. We can now close this popup. And if we go to integrations, you should see Gmail in this list of integrations. I've already tested this a few times, so I do have a few Gmail connections, but you should only have one.

## Configuring and Testing the Email Action

Back in Flowwise, simply click on refresh next to app name. And in this list, you can see all the apps that are available within Composio. Of course, we are interested in Gmail. If we refresh the auth status, this will tell us that we currently have an integration with this app. If you don't see connected here, it simply means you haven't set up the integration to that app yet. Then under actions to use, let's refresh this. And here we can see all the actions that are available to this app. So we can select the ones that we want to make available to our agent. For instance, we want to give our agent the ability to send emails. But I do want to note you are not limited to adding one action at a time. Simply click on this dropdown and add any other actions you want to include as well. I'm simply going to go with send email only. And that is really it. Let's close this. Let's save our flow. And let's try sending an email. Let's say send this information to leonfansalev@gmail.com. Our agent says this email was successfully sent. We can see the Gmail send tool was indeed called. And looking at my email, I received this one called current specials at the Oaken Barrel which contains the current specials.

## Conclusion & Future Topics

Now, of course, we've barely scratched the surface in what is possible in Flowwise, and in the next few videos, we will be exploring more complex scenarios like multi-agent teams and using state. So, if you are enjoying these videos, then hit the like button and subscribe to my channel to stay up-to-date on all the new Flowwise videos. I'll see you in the next one. Bye-bye.
